# log-fastly 0.13.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/log-fastly/0.13.0

Implementation of the [`log`] logging façade for Fastly Compute.

With this logger configured, [ log's logging statements](https://docs.rs/log#use) will send log messages to
your chosen

[Real-Time Log Streaming](https://docs.fastly.com/en/guides/about-fastlys-realtime-log-streaming-features)endpoints. You should initialize the logger as soon as your program starts. Logging statements will not do anything before initialization.

See the [Fastly
documentation](https://docs.fastly.com/en/guides/integrations#_logging-endpoints) for more
information about configuring logging endpoints for your service.

# Getting started

All you need to get started is your endpoint name and the level of log messages you want to
emit. For example, if you have an endpoint called `my_endpoint`, and you only want to emit log
messages at the "Warn" or "Error" level, you can use [`init_simple()`]:

```
log_fastly::init_simple("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Warn);
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::info!("...but this won't");
```
# Advanced configuration

For more precise control, including multiple endpoints and default endpoints for different
logging levels, use the [`Builder`] interface. The first example is equivalent to:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .init();
```
The [`Builder::max_level()`] option sets the most verbose level of logging that will be
emitted. Logging statements above that level, like `log::info!()` in the first example, will do
nothing.

**Note:** The default level is `LevelFilter::Off`, which emits no logging at all. You'll want to
change this for most configurations.

[`Builder::default_endpoint()`] sets the endpoint used whenever a logging statement is called
without a `target` field to specify its endpoint. With the default endpoint set to
`my_endpoint`, the logging statements in the first example are equivalent to:

```
log::warn!(target: "my_endpoint", "This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::info!(target: "my_endpoint", "...but this won't");
```
## Use with Compute Log Tailing

[Compute Log Tailing](https://www.fastly.com/blog/introducing-compute-edge-log-tailing-for-better-observability-and-easier-debugging) is helpful for getting debugging output quickly from a
Compute program under development by capturing output from `stdout` or `stderr`. To
configure logging to output to `stdout` or `stderr` in addition to the specified log endpoint,
enable echoing when building the logger:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .echo_stdout(true)
    .init();
```
## Multiple endpoints

Setting an endpoint as the default will automatically register it for use with the logger, but
you can register additional endpoints with [`Builder::endpoint()`]:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint("my_other_endpoint")
    .init();
log::warn!(target: "my_endpoint", "This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::warn!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "...but this will be written to my_other_endpoint");
```
## Per-endpoint logging levels

You can also set a per-endpoint logging level, though levels higher than `max_level` are always
ignored:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint_level("my_other_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Trace)
    .endpoint_level("error_only", log::LevelFilter::Error)
    .init();
log::warn!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "This will be written to my_other_endpoint...");
log::trace!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "...but this won't, because max_level wins");
log::error!(target: "error_only", "This will be written to error_only...");
log::warn!(target: "error_only", "...but this won't, because the endpoint's level is lower");
```
## Per-level default endpoints

In the previous examples, the same endpoint is set as the default for all logging levels. You
can also specify default endpoints for individual levels using
[`Builder::default_level_endpoint()`]. The defaults are combined in order, so you can specify an
overall default endpoint, and then as many level-specific endpoints as you need:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .default_level_endpoint("error_only", log::Level::Error)
    .init();
log::info!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::warn!(".. and this will too.");
log::error!("But this will be written to error_only");
```
## Module name filters

In addition to per-endpoint logging levels, you can set logging levels based on the name of the Rust module that contains the logging statement.

No filtering is done based on the module name by default, but if any module name patterns are
specified, only log statements that match one of the patterns will be emitted. For example, if
your application is a crate called `my_app`, you can filter out any messages other than
`my_app`'s :

```
# mod some_dependency { pub fn function_that_logs() {} }
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .filter_module("my_app", log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .init();
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint");
// This won't emit any log messages, because no patterns match `some_dependency`
some_dependency::function_that_logs();
```
The filter expressions support the full syntax of the [ regex](https://docs.rs/regex#syntax) crate. This is
particularly useful if your patterns overlap, but you'd like to still treat them distinctly. For
example, suppose you want to set the log level of the module

`my_app::my_module` to be more
restrictive than the top level `my_app` module. You can use `$` to make sure the
less-restrictive pattern matches to the end of the module name, instead of matching any module
name that contains `my_app`:```
mod my_module {
    pub fn do_a_thing() {
        log::warn!("This won't be written, because this module's max level is Error");
    }
}
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .filter_module("my_app$", log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .filter_module("my_app::my_module", log::LevelFilter::Error)
    .init();
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint");
// This won't emit any log messages, because "my_app$" doesn't match, and "my_app::my_module"
// is limited to Error
my_module::do_a_thing();
```
# Registering endpoints

All endpoints used by your logging statements must be registered when the logger is created. The following functions automatically register an endpoint if it is not already registered.

- [`init_simple()`]
- [`Builder::endpoint()`]
- [`Builder::endpoint_level()`]
- [`Builder::default_endpoint()`]
- [`Builder::default_level_endpoint()`]

You can pass the endpoint name as a string, or an explicit [`fastly::log::Endpoint`] value. The
following examples are equivalent:

```
log_fastly::init_simple("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Info);
```
```
log_fastly::init_simple(
    fastly::log::Endpoint::from_name("my_endpoint"),
    log::LevelFilter::Info,
);
```
If a logging statement uses `target: "my_endpoint"` but `my_endpoint` is not registered, the
message will be logged to the default endpoint for that level, if one exists.

# Endpoint and module name collisions

Due to a [limitation of  log](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/390), logging from a module with the same name as one of
your endpoints will cause logs to be sent to that endpoint, even if no

`target` is specified,
and the endpoint is not a default. For example, if you have an endpoint named `my_app`, and your
application is a crate also called `my_app`:```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint("my_app")
    .init();
log::info!("This will be written to my_app, even though my_endpoint is the default");
log::info!(
    target: "my_endpoint",
    "This will be written to my_endpoint, because the target is explicit",
);
```
We hope to address this issue in future releases, but the current workarounds are to either make sure your endpoint names and crate name are distinct, or use the explicit target syntax whenever logging from your top-level module.

[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! ```
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! ## Per-endpoint logging levels
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! You can also set a per-endpoint logging level, though levels higher than `max_level` are always
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! ignored:
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! ```no_run
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! log_fastly::Logger::builder()
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!     .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!     .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     .endpoint_level("my_other_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Trace)
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!     .endpoint_level("error_only", log::LevelFilter::Error)
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!     .init();
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! log::warn!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "This will be written to my_other_endpoint...");
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! log::trace!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "...but this won't, because max_level wins");
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! log::error!(target: "error_only", "This will be written to error_only...");
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! log::warn!(target: "error_only", "...but this won't, because the endpoint's level is lower");
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! ```
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! ## Per-level default endpoints
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! In the previous examples, the same endpoint is set as the default for all logging levels. You
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! can also specify default endpoints for individual levels using
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! [`Builder::default_level_endpoint()`]. The defaults are combined in order, so you can specify an
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! overall default endpoint, and then as many level-specific endpoints as you need:
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! ```no_run
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! log_fastly::Logger::builder()
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!     .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!     .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!     .default_level_endpoint("error_only", log::Level::Error)
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!     .init();
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! log::info!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! log::warn!(".. and this will too.");
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! log::error!("But this will be written to error_only");
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! ```
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! ## Module name filters
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! In addition to per-endpoint logging levels, you can set logging levels based on the name of the
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! Rust module that contains the logging statement.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! No filtering is done based on the module name by default, but if any module name patterns are
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! specified, only log statements that match one of the patterns will be emitted. For example, if
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! your application is a crate called `my_app`, you can filter out any messages other than
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! `my_app`'s :
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! ```no_run
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! # mod some_dependency { pub fn function_that_logs() {} }
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! log_fastly::Logger::builder()
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!     .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!     .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     .filter_module("my_app", log::LevelFilter::Warn)
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     .init();
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint");
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! // This won't emit any log messages, because no patterns match `some_dependency`
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! some_dependency::function_that_logs();
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! ```
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! The filter expressions support the full syntax of the [`regex`][regex] crate. This is
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! particularly useful if your patterns overlap, but you'd like to still treat them distinctly. For
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! example, suppose you want to set the log level of the module `my_app::my_module` to be more
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! restrictive than the top level `my_app` module. You can use `$` to make sure the
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! less-restrictive pattern matches to the end of the module name, instead of matching any module
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! name that contains `my_app`:
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! ```no_run
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! mod my_module {
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     pub fn do_a_thing() {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!         log::warn!("This won't be written, because this module's max level is Error");
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! log_fastly::Logger::builder()
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!     .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!     .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!     .filter_module("my_app$", log::LevelFilter::Warn)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     .filter_module("my_app::my_module", log::LevelFilter::Error)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!     .init();
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint");
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! // This won't emit any log messages, because "my_app$" doesn't match, and "my_app::my_module"
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! // is limited to Error
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! my_module::do_a_thing();
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! ```
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! # Registering endpoints
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! All endpoints used by your logging statements must be registered when the logger is created. The
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! following functions automatically register an endpoint if it is not already registered.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! - [`init_simple()`]
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! - [`Builder::endpoint()`]
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! - [`Builder::endpoint_level()`]
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! - [`Builder::default_endpoint()`]
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! - [`Builder::default_level_endpoint()`]
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! You can pass the endpoint name as a string, or an explicit [`fastly::log::Endpoint`] value. The
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! following examples are equivalent:
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! ```no_run
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! log_fastly::init_simple("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Info);
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! ```
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! ```no_run
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! log_fastly::init_simple(
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!     fastly::log::Endpoint::from_name("my_endpoint"),
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!     log::LevelFilter::Info,
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! );
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! ```
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! If a logging statement uses `target: "my_endpoint"` but `my_endpoint` is not registered, the
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! message will be logged to the default endpoint for that level, if one exists.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! # Endpoint and module name collisions
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! Due to a [limitation of `log`][log-issue], logging from a module with the same name as one of
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! your endpoints will cause logs to be sent to that endpoint, even if no `target` is specified,
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! and the endpoint is not a default. For example, if you have an endpoint named `my_app`, and your
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! application is a crate also called `my_app`:
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! ```no_run
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! log_fastly::Logger::builder()
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!     .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!     .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!     .endpoint("my_app")
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!     .init();
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! log::info!("This will be written to my_app, even though my_endpoint is the default");
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! log::info!(
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//!     target: "my_endpoint",
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!     "This will be written to my_endpoint, because the target is explicit",
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! );
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! ```
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//!
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! We hope to address this issue in future releases, but the current workarounds are to either make
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! sure your endpoint names and crate name are distinct, or use the explicit target syntax whenever
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! logging from your top-level module.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! [log]: https://docs.rs/log
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! [log-use]: https://docs.rs/log#use
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! [rtls]: https://docs.fastly.com/en/guides/about-fastlys-realtime-log-streaming-features
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! [regex]: https://docs.rs/regex#syntax
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! [log-issue]: https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/390
[223](https://docs.rs#223)

[241](https://docs.rs#241)};

[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)/// An implementation of the [`log::Log`] trait for Fastly Compute.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)///
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// Create and initialize a `Logger` by using the builder returned by [`Logger::builder()`].
[250](https://docs.rs#250)#[derive(Debug)]
[251](https://docs.rs#251)pub struct Logger {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// All of the endpoints that are registered with the logger.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    endpoints: HashMap<String, (Endpoint, Option<LevelFilter>)>,
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// Default endpoints for each of the log levels.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    default_endpoints: HashMap<Level, Endpoint>,
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    /// The maximum log level for all endpoints.
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    max_level: LevelFilter,
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    /// An optional matcher for each log level
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    module_filters: Option<HashMap<Level, RegexSet>>,
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// Whether to echo all log messages to `stdout`.
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    echo_stdout: bool,
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// Whether to echo all log messages to `stderr`.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    echo_stderr: bool,
[264](https://docs.rs#264)}
[265](https://docs.rs#265)
[266](https://docs.rs#266)impl Log for Logger {
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        self.lookup_endpoint(metadata, None).is_some()
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    }
[270](https://docs.rs#270)
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
[272](https://docs.rs#272)        if let Some(endpoint) = self.lookup_endpoint(record.metadata(), record.module_path()) {
[273](https://docs.rs#273)            // Collapse the formatting of the message into a single string, so that we only call the
[274](https://docs.rs#274)            // underlying `write` once. This prevents the message from being split into multiple
[275](https://docs.rs#275)            // lines in surprising ways, depending on how the format arguments are structured.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)            let mut owned = Default::default();
[277](https://docs.rs#277)            let msg = record.args().as_str().unwrap_or_else(|| {
[278](https://docs.rs#278)                owned = record.args().to_string();
[279](https://docs.rs#279)                &owned
[280](https://docs.rs#280)            });
[281](https://docs.rs#281)            // Given the type, we don't really have much of a choice about what to do if this goes
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            // wrong; panicking is probably not the right thing.
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            let _ = write!(endpoint.clone(), "{}", msg);
[284](https://docs.rs#284)            if self.echo_stdout {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)                println!("{}", msg);
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            }
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            if self.echo_stderr {
[288](https://docs.rs#288)                eprintln!("{}", msg);
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)        }
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    fn flush(&self) {}
[294](https://docs.rs#294)}
[295](https://docs.rs#295)
[296](https://docs.rs#296)impl Logger {
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    /// Get a new [`Builder`].
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    pub fn builder() -> Builder {
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        Builder::new()
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    }
[301](https://docs.rs#301)
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    fn max_level(&self) -> LevelFilter {
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        self.max_level
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    }
[305](https://docs.rs#305)
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// Look up an endpoint for a log message.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    ///
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    /// Returns `None` if no endpoint was found, or if the filter settings would prevent this
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    /// message from being emitted.
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    fn lookup_endpoint(&self, metadata: &Metadata, module_path: Option<&str>) -> Option<&Endpoint> {
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        let level = metadata.level();
[312](https://docs.rs#312)        // Immediately filter out any messages above the max level
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        if level > self.max_level {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)            return None;
[315](https://docs.rs#315)        }
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        if let Some(module_path) = module_path {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)            // If there is a module filter for this level, try to match it
[318](https://docs.rs#318)            if let Some(filter) = self.module_filters.as_ref().and_then(|fs| fs.get(&level)) {
[319](https://docs.rs#319)                if !filter.is_match(module_path) {
[320](https://docs.rs#320)                    return None;
[321](https://docs.rs#321)                }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)            }
[323](https://docs.rs#323)        }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        // If the target matches an endpoint, apply the endpoint-specific filter
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        if let Some((endpoint, filter)) = self.endpoints.get(metadata.target()) {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)            if let Some(filter) = filter {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)                if level <= *filter {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)                    Some(endpoint)
[329](https://docs.rs#329)                } else {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)                    None
[331](https://docs.rs#331)                }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)            } else {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                // If there is no filter, and the level didn't exceed the overall max, log it
[334](https://docs.rs#334)                Some(endpoint)
[335](https://docs.rs#335)            }
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        } else {
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            // For unrecognized targets, log it if there's a default endpoint for the level
[338](https://docs.rs#338)            self.default_endpoints.get(&level)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        }
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    }
[341](https://docs.rs#341)}
[342](https://docs.rs#342)
[343](https://docs.rs#343)/// A builder type for [`Logger`].
[344](https://docs.rs#344)///
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// You can use this builder to register endpoints, set default endpoints, control the levels of
[346](https://docs.rs#346)/// logging messages emitted, and filter messages based on module name.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)///
[348](https://docs.rs#348)/// A `Builder` is consumed by calling [`Builder::init()`] or [`Builder::try_init()`] to build and
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// automatically initialize the logger, or by calling [`Builder::build()`] to build the logger for
[350](https://docs.rs#350)/// manual initialization or nesting within another logger. After you call any of these methods, you
[351](https://docs.rs#351)/// can no longer call any of them on that same builder.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)#[derive(Debug)]
[353](https://docs.rs#353)pub struct Builder {
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    inner: Result<Inner, Error>,
[355](https://docs.rs#355)}
[356](https://docs.rs#356)
[357](https://docs.rs#357)#[derive(Debug)]
[358](https://docs.rs#358)struct Inner {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)    /// All of the endpoints that are registered with the logger.
[360](https://docs.rs#360)    endpoints: HashMap<String, (Endpoint, Option<LevelFilter>)>,
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    /// Default endpoints for each of the log levels.
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    default_endpoints: HashMap<Level, Endpoint>,
[363](https://docs.rs#363)    /// The maximum log level for all endpoints.
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    max_level: LevelFilter,
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// The module patterns we will match for each log level
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    module_filters: HashMap<LevelFilter, Vec<String>>,
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// Whether to echo all log messages to `stdout`.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    echo_stdout: bool,
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// Whether to echo all log messages to `stderr`.
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    echo_stderr: bool,
[371](https://docs.rs#371)}
[372](https://docs.rs#372)
[373](https://docs.rs#373)impl Default for Builder {
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    fn default() -> Self {
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        Self::new()
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    }
[377](https://docs.rs#377)}
[378](https://docs.rs#378)
[379](https://docs.rs#379)impl Builder {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// Create a new `Builder`.
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    ///
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// By default, no endpoints are registered, the maximum log level is set to `Off`, and no
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// module name filtering is done.
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    pub fn new() -> Self {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        let inner = Inner {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            endpoints: HashMap::new(),
[387](https://docs.rs#387)            default_endpoints: HashMap::new(),
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            max_level: LevelFilter::Off,
[389](https://docs.rs#389)            module_filters: HashMap::new(),
[390](https://docs.rs#390)            echo_stdout: false,
[391](https://docs.rs#391)            echo_stderr: false,
[392](https://docs.rs#392)        };
[393](https://docs.rs#393)        Self { inner: Ok(inner) }
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    }
[395](https://docs.rs#395)
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// Run a closure on the inner field, if it exists.
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    fn with_inner<F: FnOnce(&mut Inner) -> R, R>(&mut self, f: F) {
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        // It's fine not to use this result, because we're deferring errors to `build()`
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        let _ = self.inner.as_mut().map(f);
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    }
[401](https://docs.rs#401)
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// Run a closure on the inner field if it exists, and a fallible argument.
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    ///
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// If the argument is an `Err`, this replaces `inner` with that `Err`.
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    fn with_inner_and_then<A, F, R, E>(&mut self, arg: Result<A, E>, f: F)
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    where
[407](https://docs.rs#407)        F: FnOnce(&mut Inner, A) -> R,
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        E: Into<Error>,
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    {
[410](https://docs.rs#410)        match arg {
[411](https://docs.rs#411)            Ok(x) => self.with_inner(|i| f(i, x)),
[412](https://docs.rs#412)            Err(e) => self.inner = Err(e.into()),
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        }
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    }
[415](https://docs.rs#415)
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// Register an endpoint.
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    ///
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// ```no_run
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// log_fastly::Logger::builder()
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    ///     .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Trace)
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    ///     .endpoint("my_endpoint")
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    ///     .init();
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// log::info!(target: "my_endpoint", "Hello");
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// ```
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    pub fn endpoint<E>(&mut self, endpoint: E) -> &mut Self
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    where
[427](https://docs.rs#427)        E: TryInto<Endpoint>,
[428](https://docs.rs#428)        <E as TryInto<Endpoint>>::Error: Into<Error>,
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    {
[430](https://docs.rs#430)        self.with_inner_and_then(endpoint.try_into(), |i, endpoint| {
[431](https://docs.rs#431)            i.endpoints
[432](https://docs.rs#432)                .insert(endpoint.name().to_owned(), (endpoint, None))
[433](https://docs.rs#433)        });
[434](https://docs.rs#434)        self
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    }
[436](https://docs.rs#436)
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// Register an endpoint and set the maximum logging level for its messages.
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    ///
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// ```no_run
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// log_fastly::Logger::builder()

[550](https://docs.rs#550)    /// Set a logging level for modules whose names match the given [regular
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    /// expression][regex-syntax].
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    ///
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    /// By default, logging statements in any module are emitted if their level is within
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    /// [`Builder::max_level()`] and the level for their target endpoint. If you configure filters
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    /// with this method, the name of the module calling the logging statement must also match one
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    /// of the patterns, and be within the filter's specified level.
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    ///

[559](https://docs.rs#559)    /// mod my_module {
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    ///     pub fn do_a_thing() {
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    ///         log::warn!("This won't be written, because this module's max level is Error...");
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    ///         log::error!("...but this will be written");
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    ///     }
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    /// }
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    ///
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    /// log_fastly::Logger::builder()

[568](https://docs.rs#568)    ///     .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    ///     .filter_module("my_module", log::LevelFilter::Error)
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    ///     .init();
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// log::info!("This won't be written, because it's not in my_module");
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    /// // This will only emit one log message, because "my_app$" doesn't match, and
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    /// // "my_app::my_module" is limited to Error
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// my_module::do_a_thing();
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    /// ```
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    ///
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    /// [regex-syntax]: https://docs.rs/regex#syntax
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    pub fn filter_module(&mut self, regex: &str, level: LevelFilter) -> &mut Self {
[579](https://docs.rs#579)        self.with_inner(|i| {
[580](https://docs.rs#580)            i.module_filters
[581](https://docs.rs#581)                .entry(level)
[582](https://docs.rs#582)                .or_default()
[583](https://docs.rs#583)                .push(regex.to_owned())
[584](https://docs.rs#584)        });
[585](https://docs.rs#585)        self
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    }

[627](https://docs.rs#627)
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    /// Build the logger and initialize it as the global logger.
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    ///
[630](https://docs.rs#630)    /// This will fail with an `Err` value if a global logger is already initialized, or for any of
[631](https://docs.rs#631)    /// the reasons that [`Builder::build()`] can fail.
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    ///
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    /// ```no_run
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    /// # use fastly::error::Error;
[635](https://docs.rs#635)    /// # fn f() -> Result<(), Error> {
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    /// log_fastly::Builder::new()
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    ///     .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    ///     .try_init()?;
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// log::info!("Hello");
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// # Ok(()) }
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// ```
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    pub fn try_init(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error> {
[643](https://docs.rs#643)        let logger = self.build()?;
[644](https://docs.rs#644)
[645](https://docs.rs#645)        // Get the overall max level while we still own the logger
[646](https://docs.rs#646)        let max_level = logger.max_level();
[647](https://docs.rs#647)
[648](https://docs.rs#648)        // Now try to install the logger
[649](https://docs.rs#649)        let res = log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(logger));
[650](https://docs.rs#650)
[651](https://docs.rs#651)        if res.is_ok() {
[652](https://docs.rs#652)            // And finally set the max level in the global `log` state, if we successfully installed
[653](https://docs.rs#653)            // the logger
[654](https://docs.rs#654)            log::set_max_level(max_level);
[655](https://docs.rs#655)        }
[656](https://docs.rs#656)
[657](https://docs.rs#657)        res.map_err(Into::into)
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    }
[659](https://docs.rs#659)
[660](https://docs.rs#660)    /// Build a `Logger`, using up this builder.
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    ///
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// This is mainly useful if you want to manually initialize the logger, or nest it within
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    /// another [`log::Log`] implementation.
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    ///
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    /// This will fail with an `Err` value if:
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    ///
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    /// - This builder has already been used to build a `Logger`.
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    ///
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    /// - Any of the registered endpoint names are invalid.
[670](https://docs.rs#670)    ///
[671](https://docs.rs#671)    /// - Any of the module name filters set by [`Builder::filter_module()`] have invalid
[672](https://docs.rs#672)    ///   [regex syntax][regex-syntax].
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    ///
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    /// ```no_run
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    /// # fn f() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    /// let logger = log_fastly::Builder::new()
[677](https://docs.rs#677)    ///     .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    ///     .build()?;
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    /// log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(logger))?;
[680](https://docs.rs#680)    /// # Ok(()) }
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    /// ```
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    ///
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    /// [regex-syntax]: https://docs.rs/regex#syntax
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    pub fn build(&mut self) -> Result<Logger, Error> {
[685](https://docs.rs#685)        let inner = std::mem::replace(
[686](https://docs.rs#686)            &mut self.inner,
[687](https://docs.rs#687)            Err(anyhow!("Builder can only be built once")),
[688](https://docs.rs#688)        )?;
[689](https://docs.rs#689)
[690](https://docs.rs#690)        // Calculate the overall max logging level, taking into account all the endpoint-specific
[691](https://docs.rs#691)        // and default filters.
[692](https://docs.rs#692)
[693](https://docs.rs#693)        // First, find the max endpoint-specific log level.
[694](https://docs.rs#694)        let endpoint_max = inner
[695](https://docs.rs#695)            .endpoints
[696](https://docs.rs#696)            .values()
[697](https://docs.rs#697)            // If an endpoint doesn't have a filter, it's only constrained by the overall
[698](https://docs.rs#698)            // `max_level`.
[699](https://docs.rs#699)            .map(|e| e.1.unwrap_or_else(LevelFilter::max))
[700](https://docs.rs#700)            .max()
[701](https://docs.rs#701)            .unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Off);
[702](https://docs.rs#702)        // Then, find the highest log level that has a default logger.
[703](https://docs.rs#703)        let default_max = inner
[704](https://docs.rs#704)            .default_endpoints
[705](https://docs.rs#705)            .keys()
[706](https://docs.rs#706)            .max()
[707](https://docs.rs#707)            .map(Level::to_level_filter)
[708](https://docs.rs#708)            .unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Off);
[709](https://docs.rs#709)        // Take whichever of these is bigger, but then clamp it with our `max_level` which takes
[710](https://docs.rs#710)        // precedence.
[711](https://docs.rs#711)        let max_level = std::cmp::min(inner.max_level, std::cmp::max(endpoint_max, default_max));
[712](https://docs.rs#712)
[713](https://docs.rs#713)        let module_filters = generate_module_filters(inner.module_filters)?;
[714](https://docs.rs#714)
[715](https://docs.rs#715)        Ok(Logger {
[716](https://docs.rs#716)            endpoints: inner.endpoints,
[717](https://docs.rs#717)            default_endpoints: inner.default_endpoints,
[718](https://docs.rs#718)            max_level,
[719](https://docs.rs#719)            module_filters,
[720](https://docs.rs#720)            echo_stdout: inner.echo_stdout,
[721](https://docs.rs#721)            echo_stderr: inner.echo_stderr,
[722](https://docs.rs#722)        })
[723](https://docs.rs#723)    }
[724](https://docs.rs#724)}
[725](https://docs.rs#725)
[726](https://docs.rs#726)/// Build a [`RegexSet`] for each logging level from the specified filters.
[727](https://docs.rs#727)fn generate_module_filters(
[728](https://docs.rs#728)    mut regex_map: HashMap<LevelFilter, Vec<String>>,
[729](https://docs.rs#729)) -> Result<Option<HashMap<Level, RegexSet>>, Error> {
[730](https://docs.rs#730)    if regex_map.is_empty() {
[731](https://docs.rs#731)        Ok(None)
[732](https://docs.rs#732)    } else {
[733](https://docs.rs#733)        // build from highest level to lowest, extending the set as we go so that each set contains
[734](https://docs.rs#734)        // all of the regexes specified for the levels above
[735](https://docs.rs#735)        let levels = [
[736](https://docs.rs#736)            LevelFilter::Trace,
[737](https://docs.rs#737)            LevelFilter::Debug,
[738](https://docs.rs#738)            LevelFilter::Info,
[739](https://docs.rs#739)            LevelFilter::Warn,
[740](https://docs.rs#740)            LevelFilter::Error,
[741](https://docs.rs#741)        ];
[742](https://docs.rs#742)        let mut module_filters = HashMap::with_capacity(levels.len());
[743](https://docs.rs#743)        let mut running_regexes = vec![];
[744](https://docs.rs#744)        for level in levels.iter() {
[745](https://docs.rs#745)            if let Some(regexes) = regex_map.remove(level) {
[746](https://docs.rs#746)                running_regexes.extend(regexes);
[747](https://docs.rs#747)            }
[748](https://docs.rs#748)            let matcher = RegexSetBuilder::new(running_regexes.iter()).build()?;
[749](https://docs.rs#749)            let level = level
[750](https://docs.rs#750)                .to_level()
[751](https://docs.rs#751)                .expect("only iterating on LevelFilters that match a Level");
[752](https://docs.rs#752)            module_filters.insert(level, matcher);
[753](https://docs.rs#753)        }
[754](https://docs.rs#754)        Ok(Some(module_filters))
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    }
[756](https://docs.rs#756)}
[757](https://docs.rs#757)

[762](https://docs.rs#762)///

# init_simple in log_fastly - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log-fastly/0.13.0/log_fastly/fn.init_simple.html

`pub fn init_simple<E>(endpoint: E, level: `[LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.28/wasm32-wasip1/log/enum.LevelFilter.html))## Expand description

Initialize logging with a single endpoint filtered by log level.

For advanced configuration, see the [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) type, and the

[module-level documentation](https://docs.rs/index.html#advanced-configuration).

```
log_fastly::init_simple("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Warn);
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::info!("...but this won't");
```

# Builder in log_fastly - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log-fastly/0.13.0/log_fastly/struct.Builder.html

`pub struct Builder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A builder type for [ Logger](https://docs.rs/struct.Logger.html).

You can use this builder to register endpoints, set default endpoints, control the levels of logging messages emitted, and filter messages based on module name.

A `Builder` is consumed by calling [ Builder::init()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.init) or

[to build and automatically initialize the logger, or by calling](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.try_init)

`Builder::try_init()`[to build the logger for manual initialization or nesting within another logger. After you call any of these methods, you can no longer call any of them on that same builder.](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.build)

`Builder::build()`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new `Builder`.

By default, no endpoints are registered, the maximum log level is set to `Off`, and no
module name filtering is done.

Register an endpoint.

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Trace)
    .endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .init();
log::info!(target: "my_endpoint", "Hello");
```

    endpoint: E,

) -> &mut Self

Register an endpoint and set the maximum logging level for its messages.

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Trace)
    .endpoint_level("debug_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Debug)
    .init();
log::info!(target: "debug_endpoint", "This will be written to debug_endpoint...");
log::trace!(target: "debug_endpoint", "...but this won't be...");
```

#### pub fn [default_endpoint](https://docs.rs#method.default_endpoint)<E>(&mut self, endpoint: E) -> &mut Self

Set the default endpoint for all messages.

The default endpoint is used when the logging statement does not use the `target: "endpoint"` syntax.

This overrides any previous default endpoints, set either by this method or by
[ Builder::default_level_endpoint()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.default_level_endpoint).

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_level_endpoint("error_only", log::Level::Error)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint("other_endpoint")
    .init();
log::info!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::error!("...and this will too");
log::warn!(target: "other_endpoint", "This will go to other_endpoint, though");
```

Set the default endpoint for all messages of the given level.

The default endpoint is used when the logging statement does not use the `target: "endpoint"` syntax.

This overrides any previous default endpoints set for this level, either by this method or
by [ Builder::default_endpoint()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.default_endpoint).

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .default_level_endpoint("error_only", log::Level::Error)
    .endpoint("other_endpoint")
    .init();
log::info!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::error!("...but this will be written to error_only");
log::error!(target: "other_endpoint", "This will go to other_endpoint, though");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log_fastly/lib.rs.html#545-548)#### pub fn [max_level](https://docs.rs#method.max_level)(&mut self, level: [LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.28/wasm32-wasip1/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log_fastly/lib.rs.html#545-548)

#### pub fn [max_level](https://docs.rs#method.max_level)(&mut self, level: [LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.28/wasm32-wasip1/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)) -> &mut Self

Set the maximum logging level for all messages.

No messages that exceed this level will be emitted, even if a higher level is set for a specific endpoint or module name.

**Note:** The default level is `LevelFilter::Off`, which emits no logging at all. You’ll
want to change this for most configurations.

```
log_fastly::Builder::new()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .endpoint_level("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .init();
log::warn!(target: "my_endpoint", "This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::info!(target: "my_endpoint", "...but this won't");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log_fastly/lib.rs.html#578-586)#### pub fn [filter_module](https://docs.rs#method.filter_module)(&mut self, regex: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), level: [LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.28/wasm32-wasip1/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log_fastly/lib.rs.html#578-586)

#### pub fn [filter_module](https://docs.rs#method.filter_module)(&mut self, regex: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), level: [LevelFilter](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.28/wasm32-wasip1/log/enum.LevelFilter.html)) -> &mut Self

Set a logging level for modules whose names match the given [regular
expression](https://docs.rs/regex#syntax).

By default, logging statements in any module are emitted if their level is within
[ Builder::max_level()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.max_level) and the level for their target endpoint. If you configure filters
with this method, the name of the module calling the logging statement must also match one
of the patterns, and be within the filter’s specified level.

```
mod my_module {
    pub fn do_a_thing() {
        log::warn!("This won't be written, because this module's max level is Error...");
        log::error!("...but this will be written");
    }
}
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .filter_module("my_module", log::LevelFilter::Error)
    .init();
log::info!("This won't be written, because it's not in my_module");
// This will only emit one log message, because "my_app$" doesn't match, and
// "my_app::my_module" is limited to Error
my_module::do_a_thing();
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log_fastly/lib.rs.html#595-598)#### pub fn [echo_stdout](https://docs.rs#method.echo_stdout)(&mut self, enabled: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> &mut Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/log_fastly/lib.rs.html#595-598)

#### pub fn [echo_stdout](https://docs.rs#method.echo_stdout)(&mut self, enabled: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> &mut Self

Set whether all log messages should be echoed to `stdout` (`false` by default).

If this is set to `true`, all logging statements will write the message to `stdout` in
addition to the specified endpoint. This is particularly useful when debugging with
[Compute Log Tailing](https://www.fastly.com/blog/introducing-compute-edge-log-tailing-for-better-observability-and-easier-debugging).

#### pub fn [echo_stderr](https://docs.rs#method.echo_stderr)(&mut self, enabled: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> &mut Self

Set whether all log messages should be echoed to `stderr` (`false` by default).

If this is set to `true`, all logging statements will write the message to `stderr` in
addition to the specified endpoint. This is particularly useful when debugging with
[Compute Log Tailing](https://www.fastly.com/blog/introducing-compute-edge-log-tailing-for-better-observability-and-easier-debugging).

Build the logger and initialize it as the global logger.

```
log_fastly::Builder::new()
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .init();
log::info!("Hello");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

This may panic for any of the reasons that [ Builder::try_init()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.try_init) would return an error.

Build the logger and initialize it as the global logger.

This will fail with an `Err` value if a global logger is already initialized, or for any of
the reasons that [ Builder::build()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.build) can fail.

```
log_fastly::Builder::new()
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .try_init()?;
log::info!("Hello");
```
Build a `Logger`, using up this builder.

This is mainly useful if you want to manually initialize the logger, or nest it within
another [ log::Log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.28/wasm32-wasip1/log/trait.Log.html) implementation.

This will fail with an `Err` value if:

-
This builder has already been used to build a `Logger`.
-
Any of the registered endpoint names are invalid.
-
Any of the module name filters set by `Builder::filter_module()`[regex syntax](https://docs.rs/regex#syntax).

```
let logger = log_fastly::Builder::new()
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .build()?;
log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(logger))?;
```

# log_fastly - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log-fastly/latest/log_fastly/

## Expand description

Implementation of the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.28/wasm32-wasip1/log/index.html) logging façade for Fastly Compute.

With this logger configured, [ log’s logging statements](https://docs.rs/log#use) will send log messages to
your chosen

[Real-Time Log Streaming](https://docs.fastly.com/en/guides/about-fastlys-realtime-log-streaming-features)endpoints. You should initialize the logger as soon as your program starts. Logging statements will not do anything before initialization.

See the [Fastly
documentation](https://docs.fastly.com/en/guides/integrations#_logging-endpoints) for more
information about configuring logging endpoints for your service.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

All you need to get started is your endpoint name and the level of log messages you want to
emit. For example, if you have an endpoint called `my_endpoint`, and you only want to emit log
messages at the “Warn” or “Error” level, you can use [ init_simple()](https://docs.rs/fn.init_simple.html):

```
log_fastly::init_simple("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Warn);
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::info!("...but this won't");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-configuration)Advanced configuration

For more precise control, including multiple endpoints and default endpoints for different
logging levels, use the [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) interface. The first example is equivalent to:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .init();
```
The [ Builder::max_level()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.max_level) option sets the most verbose level of logging that will be
emitted. Logging statements above that level, like

`log::info!()` in the first example, will do
nothing.**Note:** The default level is `LevelFilter::Off`, which emits no logging at all. You’ll want to
change this for most configurations.

[ Builder::default_endpoint()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.default_endpoint) sets the endpoint used whenever a logging statement is called
without a

`target` field to specify its endpoint. With the default endpoint set to
`my_endpoint`, the logging statements in the first example are equivalent to:```
log::warn!(target: "my_endpoint", "This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::info!(target: "my_endpoint", "...but this won't");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-compute-log-tailing)Use with Compute Log Tailing

[Compute Log Tailing](https://www.fastly.com/blog/introducing-compute-edge-log-tailing-for-better-observability-and-easier-debugging) is helpful for getting debugging output quickly from a
Compute program under development by capturing output from `stdout` or `stderr`. To
configure logging to output to `stdout` or `stderr` in addition to the specified log endpoint,
enable echoing when building the logger:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .echo_stdout(true)
    .init();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#multiple-endpoints)Multiple endpoints

Setting an endpoint as the default will automatically register it for use with the logger, but
you can register additional endpoints with [ Builder::endpoint()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.endpoint):

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint("my_other_endpoint")
    .init();
log::warn!(target: "my_endpoint", "This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::warn!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "...but this will be written to my_other_endpoint");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#per-endpoint-logging-levels)Per-endpoint logging levels

You can also set a per-endpoint logging level, though levels higher than `max_level` are always
ignored:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint_level("my_other_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Trace)
    .endpoint_level("error_only", log::LevelFilter::Error)
    .init();
log::warn!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "This will be written to my_other_endpoint...");
log::trace!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "...but this won't, because max_level wins");
log::error!(target: "error_only", "This will be written to error_only...");
log::warn!(target: "error_only", "...but this won't, because the endpoint's level is lower");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#per-level-default-endpoints)Per-level default endpoints

In the previous examples, the same endpoint is set as the default for all logging levels. You
can also specify default endpoints for individual levels using
[ Builder::default_level_endpoint()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.default_level_endpoint). The defaults are combined in order, so you can specify an
overall default endpoint, and then as many level-specific endpoints as you need:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .default_level_endpoint("error_only", log::Level::Error)
    .init();
log::info!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::warn!(".. and this will too.");
log::error!("But this will be written to error_only");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#module-name-filters)Module name filters

In addition to per-endpoint logging levels, you can set logging levels based on the name of the Rust module that contains the logging statement.

No filtering is done based on the module name by default, but if any module name patterns are
specified, only log statements that match one of the patterns will be emitted. For example, if
your application is a crate called `my_app`, you can filter out any messages other than
`my_app`’s :

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .filter_module("my_app", log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .init();
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint");
// This won't emit any log messages, because no patterns match `some_dependency`
some_dependency::function_that_logs();
```
The filter expressions support the full syntax of the [ regex](https://docs.rs/regex#syntax) crate. This is
particularly useful if your patterns overlap, but you’d like to still treat them distinctly. For
example, suppose you want to set the log level of the module

`my_app::my_module` to be more
restrictive than the top level `my_app` module. You can use `$` to make sure the
less-restrictive pattern matches to the end of the module name, instead of matching any module
name that contains `my_app`:```
mod my_module {
    pub fn do_a_thing() {
        log::warn!("This won't be written, because this module's max level is Error");
    }
}
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .filter_module("my_app$", log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .filter_module("my_app::my_module", log::LevelFilter::Error)
    .init();
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint");
// This won't emit any log messages, because "my_app$" doesn't match, and "my_app::my_module"
// is limited to Error
my_module::do_a_thing();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#registering-endpoints)Registering endpoints

All endpoints used by your logging statements must be registered when the logger is created. The following functions automatically register an endpoint if it is not already registered.

- `init_simple()`
- `Builder::endpoint()`
- `Builder::endpoint_level()`
- `Builder::default_endpoint()`
- `Builder::default_level_endpoint()`

You can pass the endpoint name as a string, or an explicit [ fastly::log::Endpoint](https://docs.rs/fastly/0.13.0/wasm32-wasip1/fastly/log/struct.Endpoint.html) value. The
following examples are equivalent:

`log_fastly::init_simple("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Info);````
log_fastly::init_simple(
    fastly::log::Endpoint::from_name("my_endpoint"),
    log::LevelFilter::Info,
);
```
If a logging statement uses `target: "my_endpoint"` but `my_endpoint` is not registered, the
message will be logged to the default endpoint for that level, if one exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#endpoint-and-module-name-collisions)Endpoint and module name collisions

Due to a [limitation of  log](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/390), logging from a module with the same name as one of
your endpoints will cause logs to be sent to that endpoint, even if no

`target` is specified,
and the endpoint is not a default. For example, if you have an endpoint named `my_app`, and your
application is a crate also called `my_app`:```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint("my_app")
    .init();
log::info!("This will be written to my_app, even though my_endpoint is the default");
log::info!(
    target: "my_endpoint",
    "This will be written to my_endpoint, because the target is explicit",
);
```
We hope to address this issue in future releases, but the current workarounds are to either make sure your endpoint names and crate name are distinct, or use the explicit target syntax whenever logging from your top-level module.

All you need to get started is your endpoint name and the level of log messages you want to
emit. For example, if you have an endpoint called `my_endpoint`, and you only want to emit log
messages at the “Warn” or “Error” level, you can use [ init_simple()](https://docs.rs/fn.init_simple.html):

```
log_fastly::init_simple("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Warn);
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::info!("...but this won't");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-configuration)Advanced configuration

For more precise control, including multiple endpoints and default endpoints for different
logging levels, use the [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) interface. The first example is equivalent to:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .init();
```
The [ Builder::max_level()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.max_level) option sets the most verbose level of logging that will be
emitted. Logging statements above that level, like

`log::info!()` in the first example, will do
nothing.**Note:** The default level is `LevelFilter::Off`, which emits no logging at all. You’ll want to
change this for most configurations.

[ Builder::default_endpoint()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.default_endpoint) sets the endpoint used whenever a logging statement is called
without a

`target` field to specify its endpoint. With the default endpoint set to
`my_endpoint`, the logging statements in the first example are equivalent to:```
log::warn!(target: "my_endpoint", "This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::info!(target: "my_endpoint", "...but this won't");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-compute-log-tailing)Use with Compute Log Tailing

[Compute Log Tailing](https://www.fastly.com/blog/introducing-compute-edge-log-tailing-for-better-observability-and-easier-debugging) is helpful for getting debugging output quickly from a
Compute program under development by capturing output from `stdout` or `stderr`. To
configure logging to output to `stdout` or `stderr` in addition to the specified log endpoint,
enable echoing when building the logger:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .echo_stdout(true)
    .init();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#multiple-endpoints)Multiple endpoints

Setting an endpoint as the default will automatically register it for use with the logger, but
you can register additional endpoints with [ Builder::endpoint()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.endpoint):

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint("my_other_endpoint")
    .init();
log::warn!(target: "my_endpoint", "This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::warn!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "...but this will be written to my_other_endpoint");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#per-endpoint-logging-levels)Per-endpoint logging levels

You can also set a per-endpoint logging level, though levels higher than `max_level` are always
ignored:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint_level("my_other_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Trace)
    .endpoint_level("error_only", log::LevelFilter::Error)
    .init();
log::warn!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "This will be written to my_other_endpoint...");
log::trace!(target: "my_other_endpoint", "...but this won't, because max_level wins");
log::error!(target: "error_only", "This will be written to error_only...");
log::warn!(target: "error_only", "...but this won't, because the endpoint's level is lower");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#per-level-default-endpoints)Per-level default endpoints

In the previous examples, the same endpoint is set as the default for all logging levels. You
can also specify default endpoints for individual levels using
[ Builder::default_level_endpoint()](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.default_level_endpoint). The defaults are combined in order, so you can specify an
overall default endpoint, and then as many level-specific endpoints as you need:

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .default_level_endpoint("error_only", log::Level::Error)
    .init();
log::info!("This will be written to my_endpoint...");
log::warn!(".. and this will too.");
log::error!("But this will be written to error_only");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#module-name-filters)Module name filters

In addition to per-endpoint logging levels, you can set logging levels based on the name of the Rust module that contains the logging statement.

No filtering is done based on the module name by default, but if any module name patterns are
specified, only log statements that match one of the patterns will be emitted. For example, if
your application is a crate called `my_app`, you can filter out any messages other than
`my_app`’s :

```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .filter_module("my_app", log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .init();
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint");
// This won't emit any log messages, because no patterns match `some_dependency`
some_dependency::function_that_logs();
```
The filter expressions support the full syntax of the [ regex](https://docs.rs/regex#syntax) crate. This is
particularly useful if your patterns overlap, but you’d like to still treat them distinctly. For
example, suppose you want to set the log level of the module

`my_app::my_module` to be more
restrictive than the top level `my_app` module. You can use `$` to make sure the
less-restrictive pattern matches to the end of the module name, instead of matching any module
name that contains `my_app`:```
mod my_module {
    pub fn do_a_thing() {
        log::warn!("This won't be written, because this module's max level is Error");
    }
}
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .filter_module("my_app$", log::LevelFilter::Warn)
    .filter_module("my_app::my_module", log::LevelFilter::Error)
    .init();
log::warn!("This will be written to my_endpoint");
// This won't emit any log messages, because "my_app$" doesn't match, and "my_app::my_module"
// is limited to Error
my_module::do_a_thing();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#registering-endpoints)Registering endpoints

All endpoints used by your logging statements must be registered when the logger is created. The following functions automatically register an endpoint if it is not already registered.

- `init_simple()`
- `Builder::endpoint()`
- `Builder::endpoint_level()`
- `Builder::default_endpoint()`
- `Builder::default_level_endpoint()`

You can pass the endpoint name as a string, or an explicit [ fastly::log::Endpoint](https://docs.rs/fastly/0.13.0/wasm32-wasip2/fastly/log/struct.Endpoint.html) value. The
following examples are equivalent:

`log_fastly::init_simple("my_endpoint", log::LevelFilter::Info);````
log_fastly::init_simple(
    fastly::log::Endpoint::from_name("my_endpoint"),
    log::LevelFilter::Info,
);
```
If a logging statement uses `target: "my_endpoint"` but `my_endpoint` is not registered, the
message will be logged to the default endpoint for that level, if one exists.

[§](https://docs.rs#endpoint-and-module-name-collisions)Endpoint and module name collisions

Due to a [limitation of  log](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/390), logging from a module with the same name as one of
your endpoints will cause logs to be sent to that endpoint, even if no

`target` is specified,
and the endpoint is not a default. For example, if you have an endpoint named `my_app`, and your
application is a crate also called `my_app`:```
log_fastly::Logger::builder()
    .max_level(log::LevelFilter::Info)
    .default_endpoint("my_endpoint")
    .endpoint("my_app")
    .init();
log::info!("This will be written to my_app, even though my_endpoint is the default");
log::info!(
    target: "my_endpoint",
    "This will be written to my_endpoint, because the target is explicit",
);
```
We hope to address this issue in future releases, but the current workarounds are to either make sure your endpoint names and crate name are distinct, or use the explicit target syntax whenever logging from your top-level module.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_simple.html)- simple
- Initialize logging with a single endpoint filtered by log level.

# anyhow 1.0.103 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anyhow/^1.0

# Anyhow ¯\_(°ペ)_/¯

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0/anyhow/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error type
for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use Result;`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like "No such file or directory" can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use ;``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use Error;`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err;`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!;`

## No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled "std" feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow's error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Comparison to failure

The `anyhow::Error` type works something like `failure::Error`, but unlike
failure ours is built around the standard library's `std::error::Error` trait
rather than a separate trait `failure::Fail`. The standard library has adopted
the necessary improvements for this to be possible as part of [RFC 2504](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2504-fix-error.md).

## Comparison to thiserror

Use Anyhow if you don't care what error type your functions return, you just
want it to be easy. This is common in application code. Use [thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror) if you
are a library that wants to design your own dedicated error type(s) so that on
failures the caller gets exactly the information that you choose.

# log 0.4.33 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/log/^0.4.8

# log

A Rust library providing a lightweight logging *facade*.

A logging facade provides a single logging API that abstracts over the actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

## Minimum supported `rustc`

See the `rust-version` field in `Cargo.toml` for the current minimum Rust toolchain version.

This version is explicitly tested in CI and may be bumped in any release as needed. Maintaining compatibility with older compilers is a priority though, so the bar for bumping the minimum supported version is set very high. Any changes to the supported minimum version will be called out in the release notes.

## Usage

### In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided macros to
log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
```
use ;
```
### In executables

In order to produce log output, executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some options:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct [an FFI-safe wrapper over](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/421)to initialize in your libraries.`log`

- You may need to construct
- Utilities:

Executables should choose a logger implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logger implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the logger is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

## Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature, you can associate structured data with your log records:

```
use ;
```
